text:
Recommendation: move to a fixed two-week release train for both platforms, cut from a release branch on a set day, submitted to app-store review on the same day each cycle, with a staged rollout to users (phased release on iOS, staged rollout percentage on Google Play) and a standing rule that anything risky ships behind a feature flag rather than waiting for a release. Pair this with a hotfix lane that is used rarely but is pre-cleared so that it reaches users in roughly one day instead of two, and measure the whole thing with four numbers reviewed monthly.

Why two weeks: the current three-to-five-week gap is long enough that each release bundles many changes, which makes every release risky and every failure hard to trace, and it is long enough that the team's sense of readiness drifts, producing the 'when things are ready' stress. A weekly train would be ideal in principle, but with six engineers, one release manager, no QA, and a review cycle of one to three days plus occasional rejections, a weekly cadence would mean a constant review-in-flight state and frequent heroics. Two weeks gives roughly ten working days of development per cycle, enough for review to complete (budget three days, with one spare cycle of slack for a rejection) without the release manager working around the clock. The right way to judge the length is whether a normal cycle finishes without overtime; if the team is routinely missing the cut date, lengthen to three weeks rather than cutting scope silently.

The cut-off rule matters as much as the length. Every two weeks, on a fixed day, the release branch is cut from main, whatever is merged by then ships, and anything not ready is either behind a flag already merged to main or waits for the next train. Nothing is added to a branch after the cut except fixes. This removes the 'when things are ready' decision entirely, which is the main source of the stress the founders describe. The release manager's job becomes mechanical: cut, run the smoke checklist, submit, monitor, and promote the staged rollout.

Staged rollout is the main protection against the bugs users are currently seeing. Submit each build to the store as a phased or staged release, starting at a small percentage of users (for example 1 percent on Android, the phased 1 percent on iOS), hold for at least 48 hours while watching crash-free sessions, ANR or hang rates, and key funnel events, then widen. Set a rule in advance: if crash-free rate drops more than a stated threshold relative to the previous release, the rollout halts and the release manager decides between a hotfix and a rollback of the feature flags. Staged rollout works only if the team actually watches it, so the monitoring dashboard should be set up before the first train, and somebody must own the decision to widen.

Hotfix path. There are two routes that together make hotfixes faster or rarer. First, make most fixes not need a binary at all: any change that can be expressed as a server-side configuration change, a flag flip, or a remote-config value should be the default response to a problem in a newly released feature, which removes the two-day wait for those cases. Second, for the cases that do require a new binary, keep a pre-agreed hotfix lane: a short branch from the live release tag, a reduced checklist, and a standing agreement that the team will submit it to review the same day it is ready rather than waiting for the next train. The realistic target is that a true binary hotfix reaches users in about one day, with review being the main variable; the team should not promise faster than the store allows. The expectation is that hotfixes drop from about one in four releases to something closer to one in ten, mostly because flags absorb the problems that used to need a new build.

Feature flag rule. A change goes behind a flag when any of the following is true: it changes a user-visible flow or data model; it touches payments, authentication, or anything that is expensive to get wrong; it depends on a backend change that may ship on a different schedule; or it is large enough that it would not fit in a single cycle with review. A change ships without a flag when it is a bug fix, copy or visual tweak with no behaviour change, internal refactoring covered by tests, or a change so small that turning it off would be more work than the change itself. Every flag needs an owner and an expiry date, and flags older than one release cycle after full rollout are removed; without that discipline flags become a second source of complexity that makes the app harder to reason about.

Caveats and open questions. Flags add code paths and need testing in both states, which costs engineering time that the team must budget; the first cycle will be slower. The store review process is outside the team's control, so the cadence will occasionally slip by a cycle when a build is rejected, and the release manager needs a documented procedure for rejections rather than improvising. Staged rollout percentages are only useful if the user base is large enough that a small percentage yields a signal within 48 hours; if daily active users are small, the threshold rules should be based on absolute event counts rather than percentages, and the team should check this in the first month. Finally, the release manager role is a single point of failure, so a second engineer should shadow each cycle and be able to run it.

Measuring success in three months. Track four numbers on a shared sheet, reviewed in a fifteen-minute slot each cycle. First, cadence: the share of planned release dates hit within three days; target at least 80 percent. Second, hotfix rate: the share of releases followed by a binary hotfix; baseline about 25 percent, target 10 percent or lower. Third, time to user for a hotfix: measured from the decision to the percentage of users on the fixed build; baseline about two days, target about one. Fourth, incident exposure: the share of users affected by crashes or regressions from a release before a halt, which the staged rollout should keep low; set a baseline from the next two releases and aim to reduce it. Add one qualitative check: a short survey of the team after six cycles asking whether releases feel routine. If the cadence and hotfix numbers have moved and the team reports less stress, keep the process; if the cadence is slipping, lengthen the train to three weeks; if hotfix rate has not dropped, look first at which problems still required binaries and whether flags were skipped when they should have been used.
